name: Zipoy-Voorhees Deformed Mass
description: A static, axially symmetric vacuum field whose Weyl potential is Newton's potential of a uniform rod, found by Georges Darmois in 1927, David Zipoy in 1966, and B. H. Voorhees in 1970, and also called the $\gamma$ metric and the $q$ metric. It deforms Schwarzschild's metric by a quadrupole, and for every deformation a naked curvature singularity stands where the horizon was.
convention: The parameter $m$ is a length, and the mass $M$ has $GM/c^2 = \delta m$ with $\delta = 1 + q$. We keep factors of $c$ explicit, and the Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$.
history: The Zipoy-Voorhees metric belongs to Hermann Weyl's class of static, axially symmetric vacuum fields, as the Curzon-Chazy particle and Levi-Civita's cylinder do [weyl1917, bicak2000, herrera1999]. Its potential $\psi$ is the Newtonian potential of a uniform rod of length $2m$ and mass per unit length $\delta/2$ lying on the axis [herrera1999, bicak2000]. Georges Darmois found the solution in 1927 [richterek2002]. David Zipoy solved the vacuum equations in oblate and prolate spheroidal coordinates in 1966, and his prolate solutions contain "a line singularity of finite length" [zipoy1966]. B. H. Voorhees wrote the metric in the prolate spheroidal coordinates $x$ and $y$ in 1970, with $g_{tt} = -\left((x - 1)/(x + 1)\right)^\delta$ [voorhees1970, kodamahikida2003]. Paul Esposito and Louis Witten wrote $\gamma$ for $\delta$ in 1975, the origin of the name $\gamma$ metric [esposito1975, lukes2012].¶The mass of the spacetime is $M = \delta m$, and at $\delta = 1$ the metric is Schwarzschild's, whose rod has length $2M$ [kodamahikida2003, bicak2000]. The surfaces of constant $g_{tt}$ are prolate for $0 < \delta < 1$ and oblate for $\delta > 1$ [kodamahikida2003]. Hernando Quevedo set $\delta = 1 + q$ in 2011, in coordinates that are Schwarzschild's at $q = 0$, and computed Robert Geroch's multipole moments of the metric [quevedo2011]. The monopole is $M_0 = (1 + q)m$ and the quadrupole is $M_2 = -m^3q(1 + q)(2 + q)/3$, and every higher moment is a function of these two [quevedo2011]. With $\delta \to \infty$ and $m \to 0$ at fixed $\delta m$ the metric becomes that of the Curzon-Chazy particle [herrera1999]. Luis Herrera, Filipe Paiva, and Nilton Santos showed in 1999 that as $m \to \infty$ it becomes, locally, Levi-Civita's metric with $\sigma = \delta/2$ [herrera1999].¶Werner Israel proved in 1967 that among static, asymptotically flat vacuum spacetimes with closed, simply connected surfaces of constant $g_{tt}$, Schwarzschild's is "the only one which has a nonsingular infinite-red-shift surface" [israel1967]. For every $\delta$ other than $0$ and $1$ the curvature diverges on the rod, which is the surface $r = 2m$ in Quevedo's coordinates, and no horizon surrounds it [kodamahikida2003, quevedo2011]. K. S. Virbhadra found in 1996 that for $\delta < 1$ the singularity is visible from infinity along the axis and in the equatorial plane, and that for $\delta > 1$ it is visible in the plane and invisible along the axis, which he called "directional nakedness" [virbhadra1996]. Demetrios Papadopoulos, Bob Stewart, and Louis Witten recognized in 1981 that each end of the rod is a hypersurface which the coordinates collapse to a point [papadopoulos1981, kodamahikida2003]. Hideo Kodama and Wataru Hikida showed in 2003 that the singularity is "point-like for $\delta<0$, string-like for $0<\delta<1$ and ring-like for $\delta>1$", and that for $\delta > 0$ its Komar mass is positive [kodamahikida2003]. For $\delta = 2$, $\delta = 3$, and $\delta \geq 4$ they extended the spacetime across the ends of the rod and found a degenerate Killing horizon with a ring singularity in the equatorial plane [kodamahikida2003].¶Akira Tomimatsu and Humitaka Sato published in 1972 a rotating vacuum solution that reduces to Kerr's metric at one value of its angular momentum and to a Weyl metric at zero angular momentum [tomimatsu1972]. The static limits of their family are the Zipoy-Voorhees metrics of integer $\delta$ [kodamahikida2003]. Saken Toktarbay and Quevedo gave a rotating generalization for every $q$ in 2014, with independent parameters for the mass, the quadrupole, and the angular momentum [toktarbay2014]. Jeandrew Brink integrated geodesics of the Zipoy-Voorhees metric numerically in 2008, found no sign of chaos, and conjectured a fourth constant of the motion, quartic in the momenta [brink2008, lukes2012]. Georgios Lukes-Gerakopoulos found chaotic layers and Birkhoff chains in the phase space of the geodesics in 2012 [lukes2012]. Andrzej Maciejewski, Maria Przybylska, and Tomasz Stachowiak proved in 2013 that the geodesic motion has no further first integral meromorphic in the phase space variables, so it is not Liouville integrable [maciejewski2013].¶Anirban Chowdhury, Mandar Patil, Daniele Malafarina, and Pankaj Joshi divided the circular geodesics of the equatorial plane into three regimes in 2012 [chowdhury2012]. For $\delta > 1/2$ a photon sphere surrounds the singularity, and the stable circular orbits run from a radius outside it to infinity [chowdhury2012]. For $1/\sqrt{5} < \delta < 1/2$ there is no photon sphere, and the stable orbits fill two regions separated by a band of unstable ones, the inner region reaching the singularity [chowdhury2012]. For $\delta < 1/\sqrt{5}$ the circular orbits are stable from infinity down to the singularity [chowdhury2012]. Askar Abdikamalov, Ahmadjon Abdujabbarov, Dimitry Ayzenberg, Malafarina, Cosimo Bambi, and Bobomurat Ahmedov traced light rays through the metric in 2019 and computed its shadow [abdikamalov2019]. They found the shadow hard to tell from Schwarzschild's for $\delta$ near $1$ and clearly distinguishable for $\delta < 1/2$ [abdikamalov2019].

related.text: The undeformed case, $q = 0$, whose rod has length $r_s$ [bicak2000].
The Weyl field of an infinite line of mass, which the rod approaches locally as $m \to \infty$ [herrera1999].
The rod shrunk to a point at fixed mass, the limit $q \to \infty$ and $m \to 0$ with $(1 + q)m$ fixed [herrera1999].
The same $g_{tt} = -f^{\delta}$ on a spacetime that stays spherical and pays for it with a massless scalar field. It too has a naked singularity where Schwarzschild's horizon was [chowdhury2012].

The rotating black hole. Tomimatsu and Sato's spinning solution of 1972 is Kerr's metric at one value of its angular momentum, and the static limits of their family are the Zipoy-Voorhees metrics of whole number $\delta$ [tomimatsu1972, kodamahikida2003].

parameters.description: Half the length of the rod in Weyl's coordinates, a length; the mass $M$ at spatial infinity has $GM/c^2 = (1 + q)m$
Quadrupole parameter, dimensionless, $q > -1$; $q = 0$ is Schwarzschild's metric, and the quadrupole moment is $M_2 = -m^3q(1 + q)(2 + q)/3$, prolate for $q < 0$ and oblate for $q > 0$
Schwarzschild's function; Weyl's potential is $\psi = \tfrac{1}{2}(1 + q)\ln f$
Weyl's second function is $\gamma = -\tfrac{1}{2}(1 + q)^2\ln h$; $h = 1$ on the axis

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$ that are Schwarzschild's at $q = 0$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $r$ a length, and write $f = 1 - 2m/r$ and $h = 1 + m^2\sin^2\theta/(r^2 - 2mr)$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

coordinates.name: Prolate spheroidal

parameters.description: Half the length of the rod in Weyl's coordinates, a length; the mass $M$ at spatial infinity has $GM/c^2 = \delta m$
Deformation parameter, dimensionless, $\delta = 1 + q > 0$; $\delta/2$ is the mass per unit length of the rod in Weyl's potential, and $\delta = 1$ is Schwarzschild's metric
Schwarzschild's function $1 - 2m/r$; Weyl's potential is $\psi = \tfrac{1}{2}\delta\ln f$
Weyl's second function is $\gamma = -\tfrac{1}{2}\delta^2\ln h$; $h = 1$ on the axis $y = \pm 1$

coordinates.convention: We use prolate spheroidal coordinates $(t, x, y, \phi)$, with $x = r/m - 1$ and $y = \cos\theta$ dimensionless and $t$ carrying dimensions of time, and write $f = (x - 1)/(x + 1)$ and $h = (x^2 - y^2)/(x^2 - 1)$. Weyl's canonical coordinates are $\rho = m\sqrt{(x^2 - 1)(1 - y^2)}$ and $z = mxy$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

nonzero.value: \dfrac{\delta\left(1 - y^2\right)\left(\delta^2\,x\left(1 - y^2\right) - 2\delta\left(x^2 - y^2\right) + x\left(2x^2 - 1 - y^2\right)\right)h^{\delta^2}}{\left(x^2 - y^2\right)^2}

coordinates.kretschmann: K = \dfrac{16\delta^2\left(\delta^4\left(1 - y^2\right) - 3\delta^3\,x\left(1 - y^2\right) + \delta^2\left(6x^2 - 2 - 3x^2\,y^2 - y^2\right) - 3\delta\,x\left(2x^2 - 1 - y^2\right) + 3x^4 - 3x^2 + 1 - y^2\right)f^{2\delta}h^{2\delta^2}}{m^4\left(x^2 - 1\right)^2\left(x^2 - y^2\right)^3}

geodesics: \ddot{x} + \dfrac{\delta\,f^{2\delta}h^{\delta^2}}{m^2\left(x^2 - y^2\right)}\dot{t}^2 + \dfrac{\delta^2\,x\left(1 - y^2\right) - \delta\left(x^2 - y^2\right) - x\left(1 - y^2\right)}{\left(x^2 - 1\right)\left(x^2 - y^2\right)}\dot{x}^2 + \dfrac{2y\left(\delta^2 - 1\right)}{x^2 - y^2}\dot{x}\dot{y} - \dfrac{\delta^2\,x\left(1 - y^2\right) - \delta\left(x^2 - y^2\right) + x\left(x^2 - 1\right)}{\left(1 - y^2\right)\left(x^2 - y^2\right)}\dot{y}^2 + \dfrac{\left(1 - y^2\right)\left(x^2 - 1\right)\left(\delta - x\right)h^{\delta^2}}{x^2 - y^2}\dot{\phi}^2 = 0
